overview: Both describe the geometry of double bonds in unsaturated fatty acids, with very different health implications.
genZNote: Cis fats: naturally bent and healthier. Trans fats: artificially straightened and the ones your cardiologist worries about.

aspects.label: Molecular Geometry
aspects.valueA: Hydrogen atoms on the same side of the double bond, creating a bent shape.
aspects.valueB: Hydrogen atoms on opposite sides of the double bond, creating a straighter shape closer to saturated fat.

aspects.label: Common Source
aspects.valueA: Naturally occurring in most plant oils and fish.
aspects.valueB: Formed by partial hydrogenation of vegetable oils; found in many processed/fried foods.

aspects.label: Health Effect
aspects.valueA: Generally considered healthier when consumed in moderation.
aspects.valueB: Raises LDL ('bad') cholesterol and lowers HDL, increasing heart disease risk.

overlay.examHighYieldNote: Trans fats are the main dietary fat type actively linked to increased cardiovascular disease risk, prompting many countries to restrict them.
overlay.memoryTrick: Cis = 'same side', bent, natural. Trans = 'across', straight, man-made mostly.
overlay.commonMisconception: Not all trans fats are man-made — a small amount occurs naturally in the meat and dairy of ruminant animals.
